title: Out of the Whirlwind
subtitle: Job in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Job is the Bible's long, honest argument with suffering. A good man loses everything, sits in the ashes, and refuses both to curse God and to accept his friends' tidy explanations. Then God speaks out of the storm, and Job says, I had heard of you, but now I see you.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. Where Job grieves, the poems grieve with him; they do not explain his pain away.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open Job alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word. If you are carrying something heavy as you read, please don't carry it alone.

paintings.title: there was a man
paintings.epigraph: “That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil.”
paintings.poem:
the story starts
like a fairy tale:
there was a man.

good.
honest.
seven sons, three daughters,
flocks on every hill.

and every morning
he got up early
and prayed for his children,
just in case.

remember him like this.
the book is about to take
everything else away.

paintings.title: behind the scenes
paintings.epigraph: “Have you considered my servant, Job?”
paintings.poem:
behind the scenes,
a conversation
Job never hears.

does he serve you for nothing?
take it all away,
and see.

the book never tells Job
about this chapter.

he has to suffer
without the explanation.

most of us do.

paintings.title: on his face
paintings.epigraph: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there.”
paintings.poem:
four messengers,
one after another,
each still speaking
when the next arrived.

the oxen. the sheep.
the camels.
and then—
the children.

and Job tore his robe,
shaved his head,
fell to the ground,
and worshiped.

the Lord gave.
the Lord has taken away.

it isn't a formula.
it's a man on his face,
still talking to God.

paintings.title: the ash heap
paintings.epigraph: “He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.”
paintings.poem:
sores from head to foot.

he sat on the ash heap
outside the town,
where they burned the refuse,
scraping himself
with a broken piece of pot.

the greatest man in the east,
sitting in the dump.

no one should have to
sit there alone.

paintings.title: the hard too
paintings.epigraph: “Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?”
paintings.poem:
his wife said: give up.
curse God and die.

don't be too hard on her.
she had lost
ten children too.

and Job said:
we take the good from God.
shouldn't we take the hard too?

not a theory of suffering.
a man refusing
to let go of the hand.

paintings.title: seven days
paintings.epigraph: “no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.”
paintings.poem:
his three friends came
and didn't recognize him.

they wept.
they tore their robes.
they threw dust on their heads.

and then
they sat with him
on the ground
seven days and seven nights,
and said nothing.

this was the best thing
they would do
in the whole book.

sometimes the kindest words
are none.

paintings.title: the day I was born
paintings.epigraph: “Let the day perish in which I was born”
paintings.poem:
when he finally spoke,
he cursed the day he was born.

the Bible doesn't rush him.
it gives him
a whole chapter.

some pain is so deep
that wishing you'd never been
feels like the only honest prayer.

Job brought even that
to God,
out loud,
among friends.

if you've ever felt it,
don't carry it alone.
say it to God,
and to someone who will sit with you.

paintings.title: what I feared
paintings.epigraph: “For the thing which I fear comes on me”
paintings.poem:
the thing I feared most
came.

no ease.
no quiet.
no rest.
only trouble.

the worst-case scenario
isn't only a nightmare.
sometimes it happens.

and God
is still God
on the other side of it.
the book isn't over.

paintings.title: you used to hold others up
paintings.epigraph: “Your words have supported him who was falling”
paintings.poem:
Eliphaz begins
with something true:

you used to hold others up.
your words
steadied the ones who were falling.

and now it's you.

it's harder
to receive comfort
than to give it—
harder still
when the comforters
start explaining.

paintings.title: sparks
paintings.epigraph: “man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.”
paintings.poem:
sparks fly upward.
trouble comes.
it's just how things are.

true enough.

but the friends
kept going:
so you must have done
something to deserve this.

that part
was wrong.

the whole book
is an argument
with that one idea.

paintings.title: kindness
paintings.epigraph: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend”
paintings.poem:
a man ready to faint
needs kindness from his friends—

even if he's lost his grip on faith,
Job says.

not a lecture.
not a theology.
kindness.

the friend who shows up
with water
does more
than the friend who shows up
with answers.

paintings.title: the shuttle
paintings.epigraph: “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.”
paintings.poem:
the shuttle flies
across the loom—
back, forth,
back, forth,
faster than you can follow.

my days are like that,
Job says,
and running out of thread.

he isn't being dramatic.
he's being honest.
God can handle
honest.

paintings.title: someone in the middle
paintings.epigraph: “There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.”
paintings.poem:
God isn't a man like me,
that I could argue my case.

if only there were someone
in the middle—

someone to put one hand on God,
and one hand on me.

Job didn't know it,
but he was describing
someone who would come.

paintings.title: ask the animals
paintings.epigraph: “But ask the animals, now, and they will teach you; the birds of the sky, and they will tell you.”
paintings.poem:
you want wisdom?
ask the animals.
ask the birds.
ask the fish in the sea.

they know
who holds them.

in his hand
is the life of every living thing,
and the breath
of every person.

including mine,
even now,
even here.

paintings.title: to his face
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, he will kill me. I have no hope. Nevertheless, I will maintain my ways before him.”
paintings.poem:
even if he kills me,
I'll still stand here
and make my case to his face.

that's not unbelief.
it's the opposite.

you only argue
with someone
you're sure is there,
and sure is listening.

paintings.title: at the scent of water
paintings.epigraph: “that it will sprout again, that the tender branch of it will not cease.”
paintings.poem:
cut down a tree,
and there's hope—
at the scent of water
it will bud again.

but a man?
lie down, and he doesn't rise.

Job asks the question
and can't answer it:
if a man dies,
will he live again?

the rest of the Bible
has been answering
ever since.

paintings.title: miserable comforters
paintings.epigraph: “Y ou are all miserable comforters!”
paintings.poem:
I could talk like you,
Job says,
if you were in my place.

I could shake my head,
string words together.

but I would strengthen you
with my mouth.
I'd ease your pain.

some comfort
makes it worse.

before you explain someone's suffering,
sit down
and be quiet a while.

paintings.title: my witness
paintings.epigraph: “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven.”
paintings.poem:
even now,
with everyone against me,
my witness
is in heaven.

someone up there
knows the truth
and will speak for me.

when every voice on earth
has already decided,
there's one
who hasn't.

paintings.title: cut in rock
paintings.epigraph: “That with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!”
paintings.poem:
oh, that my words
were written down—

cut into rock
with an iron pen,
filled with lead,
forever.

he thought no one would remember.

and here they are,
still being read
thousands of years later.

he got his wish.

paintings.title: I know
paintings.epigraph: “After my skin is destroyed, then I will see God in my flesh”
paintings.poem:
in the middle of the worst,
out of nowhere,
the highest line in the book:

I know
that my Redeemer lives.

and in the end
he will stand on the earth.

and I will see him,
with my own eyes—
I, and not another.

he didn't know how.
he knew who.

paintings.title: where to find him
paintings.epigraph: “Oh that I knew where I might find him!”
paintings.poem:
if only I knew where to find him—

I go east. not there.
west. can't find him.
north. south.
nothing.

sometimes God
feels impossible to find.

the Bible
doesn't pretend otherwise.

paintings.title: like gold
paintings.epigraph: “When he has tried me, I will come out like gold.”
paintings.poem:
I can't find him.

but—
he knows the way I'm taking.

I don't see him.
he sees me.

and when this fire is done,
I'll come out
like gold.

paintings.title: the fringe
paintings.epigraph: “How small a whisper do we hear of him!”
paintings.poem:
the heavens,
the deep,
the boundary of the sea—

all of it,
Job says,
is only
the fringe of his ways.

a whisper.

we hear
the faintest whisper.
imagine
the thunder.

paintings.title: the mine
paintings.epigraph: “But where will wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?”
paintings.poem:
men dig for silver,
cut shafts into the dark,
hang on ropes,
turn mountains over
looking for gold and sapphires.

but wisdom?

you can't mine it.
you can't buy it.
the deep says:
it isn't in me.

paintings.title: here it is
paintings.epigraph: “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.”
paintings.poem:
God knows the way to it.
he saw it when he made the wind
and the rain.

and he said to us:
here it is.

awe of the Lord—
that's wisdom.
turning from evil—
that's understanding.

not hidden in the rock.
right here,
on your knees.

paintings.title: eyes to the blind
paintings.epigraph: “I was eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.”
paintings.poem:
Job remembers
the old days:

I rescued the poor who cried.
the orphan.
the widow.

I was eyes for the blind,
feet for the lame,
a father to the needy.

it's not a boast.
it's a picture
of the life
God still calls good.

paintings.title: no answer
paintings.epigraph: “I cry to you, and you do not answer me.”
paintings.poem:
I cry to you.
you don't answer.

I stand up.
you just look at me.

if you've prayed like this,
you're in the Bible.

God kept this line
too.

paintings.title: signed
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!”
paintings.poem:
here's my signature.
let God answer me.

Job signs his case
and sets it down.

the words of Job
are ended.

he's said everything.
now
he waits.

paintings.title: borrowed breath
paintings.epigraph: “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.”
paintings.poem:
a young man, Elihu,
has been waiting to speak.

and some of what he says
is true:

God's Spirit made me.
the breath of the Almighty
gives me life.

every breath you're taking
while you read this—
borrowed
from him.

paintings.title: songs in the night
paintings.epigraph: “who gives songs in the night”
paintings.poem:
where is God my Maker,
who gives songs in the night?

not songs
after the night.

in it.

paintings.title: stand still
paintings.epigraph: “Stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God.”
paintings.poem:
stop, Job.
stand still.

look at the lightning.
the snow.
the clouds balanced in the sky.

before God speaks,
the storm
is already coming.

paintings.title: God speaks
paintings.epigraph: “Then Yahweh answered Job out of the whirlwind”
paintings.poem:
thirty-five chapters of talking.

and then
God speaks.

not in a whisper.
out of the storm.

he doesn't explain the suffering.
he doesn't mention
the conversation in chapter one.

he shows up.

and for Job,
that turns out
to be the answer.

paintings.title: the morning stars
paintings.epigraph: “when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?”
paintings.poem:
where were you
when I laid the earth's foundations?

when I measured it,
stretched the line,
set the cornerstone—

while the morning stars sang together
and heaven shouted for joy?

it isn't an insult.
it's an invitation
to see
how big the world is,
and who is holding it.

paintings.title: where I keep the snow
paintings.epigraph: “Have you entered the treasuries of the snow”
paintings.poem:
have you seen
where I keep the snow?
the storehouses of hail?

who fathered the rain?
who gave birth to the frost?

God takes Job on a tour
of the weather,

and every question means:
I've been taking care of all this.
I can take care of you.

paintings.title: Orion
paintings.epigraph: “Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades, or loosen the cords of Orion?”
paintings.poem:
can you tie the Pleiades together?
loosen Orion's belt?

the same stars
Job looked at.
the same stars
you can see tonight.

go outside.
look up.
he's still asking.

paintings.title: not your job
paintings.epigraph: “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk soars, and stretches her wings toward the south?”
paintings.poem:
the wild donkey.
the ostrich.
the horse that laughs at fear.
the hawk
stretching her wings toward the south.

God knows them all,
feeds them all,
delights in them all.

not one of them
is Job's job.

that's a kind of rest.

paintings.title: hand on my mouth
paintings.epigraph: “I lay my hand on my mouth.”
paintings.poem:
Job had demanded a hearing.
now he has one.

and he says:
I'm small.
what could I answer?
I lay my hand on my mouth.

sometimes the end of the argument
isn't losing.

it's seeing
who you were arguing with.

paintings.title: now I see
paintings.epigraph: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.”
paintings.poem:
I had heard of you.
now I see you.

that's what the whole book
was for.

not an explanation.
a meeting.

Job's questions were never answered.

they were
outgrown.

paintings.title: for his friends
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends.”
paintings.poem:
God told the friends:
you haven't spoken rightly of me,
as my servant Job has.

the angry, honest man—
right.
the tidy explainers—
wrong.

and then the turn,
the moment everything changed:

when he prayed
for his friends,

the ones who hurt him most.

paintings.title: full of days
paintings.epigraph: “So Job died, being old and full of days.”
paintings.poem:
the Lord blessed
the latter part of his life
more than the first.

sons and daughters again,
and he named his daughters himself:
Dove, Cinnamon,
Horn of Eye-paint,

and gave them an inheritance
alongside their brothers.

it doesn't erase the grief.
nothing could.

but he died
old,
and full of days.
